sections.content: Data has always captured my interest, how to visualize it, communicate it, understand it. Building my [portfolio](/portfolio-website-svelte), I worked with this interest directly: Instead of relying on a CMS like WordPress, I built the site in Svelte as a fully data-driven system where projects are structured in JSON and can be searched/filtered by tags, tools, or programming languages. Designing the site this way made me realize how much the structure of data shapes how information can be explored. The [Data Physicalization Project](/physical-data) (\ref{data-physicalization-museum}) revealed another dimension of data. My team created a museum installation translating planetary datasets into physical interactions using 3D-printed planets, mechanical dials, and temperature output. Those mappings made me aware that analytically correct data is not automatically experientially meaningful. What matters is how variables are translated into forms that people can intuitively interpret. The [M12 study](/digital-twin-in-education) (\ref{m12}) required engaging with data from a research perspective. I conducted a mixed pre/post experiment with 41 participants testing whether feedback style affected novice programmers' confidence. Running the analysis required actually understanding what a mixed-design ANOVA measures rather than simply using statistical software. Looking back across projects, I also noticed that my engagement with AI and machine learning often remains at the application layer, integrating OCR pipelines, LLM APIs, or computer vision, rather than exploring those systems in depth. Becoming aware of that pattern made me more conscious of the difference between using advanced tools and understanding them. Level: advanced. I can use data and machine learning meaningfully in a system, with the honesty that my depth still sits closer to the application layer than the theory (adressed this in FMP however).
